title: Four schools
hook: Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya, Gelug: later years explain each, never ranked

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sand mandala, built grain by grain, then poured into the river. Your line: swept away. Today closes the week.

Some of the great rivers of Asia begin on the Tibetan plateau. Same snow, same high ground, and then they run off through different valleys, feeding different fields, each one a whole river. Tibetan Buddhism is a little like that. Visit four of its monasteries and you may hear four styles of chanting and meet four lines of teachers going back centuries. Today: the four schools, just their names and a first glance.
screen: `RIVERS FROM THE SAME HIGH GROUND.` → `DIFFERENT VALLEYS, WHOLE RIVERS.` → `FOUR MONASTERIES, FOUR STYLES.`

segments.voice: Nyingma means the old ones. It carries the early translations from the time of Padmasambhava, and it's known for a teaching called dzogchen, the great perfection. Kagyu means the lineage of the spoken word. It runs from Marpa the translator to his student Milarepa, the poet who lived in mountain caves, to Gampopa, whose book gave you the four thoughts. Its best-known teaching is mahamudra, the great seal. Sakya is named for the gray earth where its first monastery was built, and one family, the Khön, has guided it for generations. Its central teaching is called the path and its fruit. Gelug means the virtuous ones. It grew from the scholar Tsongkhapa and his students, with a strong emphasis on monastic discipline, study and debate; the Dalai Lamas come from this school. What they share: the same monastic code, the Mahayana heart of bodhicitta, the Vajrayana tools of mantra and visualization. They differ in lineage, in emphasis, in which texts come first. Later, a movement called Rime, meaning without sides, urged Tibetans to learn from all of them. And alongside the four lives Bön, Tibet's own old religious tradition, with lineages of its own. Later years will open each school properly. For now, the names, and no ranking. Looking back at the week: check the teacher. Take in, send out. One slogan. For all of us. She comes quickly. Swept away. And today: four streams.
screen: `NYINGMA — THE OLD ONES.` · `KAGYU — THE SPOKEN LINEAGE.` · `SAKYA — THE GRAY EARTH.` · `GELUG — THE VIRTUOUS ONES.` · then, large: `FOUR STREAMS.`

segments.voice: Name the four slowly, one per breath, Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya, Gelug, and picture four rivers leaving the same snowfield. Then let the names go and sit with the breath, the same breath whichever valley you're in. When the mind wanders, come back to the high, quiet ground.
Four schools. Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug: four lineages of Tibetan Buddhism, sharing one heart, each a whole way.
Your line: four streams. One high ground, many valleys, each a whole river. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists usually practice within one of the four schools, Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya or Gelug, through a particular teacher and monastery, and many also receive teachings from other schools in the nonsectarian spirit of the Rime movement.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed 'four different hats' from the hook (inaccurate: the Gelug are the 'yellow hats', while Nyingma, Kagyu and Sakya are broadly 'red hat' schools, so there are not four hats); hook no longer opens 'Walk into'; cut 'eighth century', 'eleventh century', 'around six hundred years ago' and 'nineteenth century' from the voice and myth (dates not in the cited text); 'earliest translations' softened to 'early translations'; named the Khön family; Gelug 'founded by Tsongkhapa' reworded to 'grew from Tsongkhapa and his students'.
Sakya's first monastery founded 1073 by Khön Könchok Gyalpo; given as 'the eleventh century'.
Kagyu glossed as 'lineage of the spoken word' (bka' brgyud; bka' is often rendered 'command' or 'oral instruction'): confirm.
Bön mentioned beside the four without ranking; Keeper may prefer different wording on Bön's relation to Buddhism.
